analysis.title: THINK Ahead: This is how bad European inflation could get this winter
key_insights: Natural gas prices keep hitting new highs, and oil and gas have both eclipsed the ECB's 'adverse' scenario from its September projections. What began as an oil crisis is becoming a gas crisis, and the rise in percentage terms is larger than at the equivalent point of the 2022 Ukraine shock.
ING says 4% eurozone inflation this winter increasingly looks baked in. Eurozone inflation was 3.8% in September and UK inflation was 3.5%.

UK household energy bills are expected to rise about 25% in January under the price cap. By next summer the energy category is likely to add roughly a percentage point more to inflation than it does today. Eurozone household energy prices tend to follow a similar pattern.

The oil price spike earlier this year starts dropping out of the annual comparison from April, offsetting some of the gas effect. ING says this probably will not be enough to bring inflation back to 2% by spring or early summer.
Reaching 5% eurozone inflation needs another leg higher in energy. Oil at $130/bbl with gas staying at current levels would roughly get there, per ING's scenario analysis.

Eurozone consumer food inflation is only 1.1%, against a peak near 20% in the last episode. Fresh food picked up in September, driven by fruit-bearing vegetables, while import and producer food prices are still in deflation. ING expects this to change, and October inflation data due late next week is the main thing to watch. The ECB sees food inflation peaking near 3.5% next summer.

Second-round effects in energy-intensive inflation categories show no sign of pressure so far. They tend to lag energy inflation by about six months, so effects should start to appear now. Upside risks are AI investment bottlenecks, a resurgence in the jobs market and widespread government energy support packages.
The correlation between oil prices and two-year swap rates has broken down since mid-September, when the French political and fiscal turmoil began.

The ECB is expected to stay on hold at its October meeting because of the French fiscal and political crisis and higher bond yields. The next hike decision is delayed to December. The agenda also includes whether to curtail the hiking cycle or stop quantitative tightening, and the future of ECB President Lagarde.

ING's base case is that second-round effects will not materialise at scale. It does not forecast further ECB hikes next year and sees a possible cut by next Christmas. A December hike would be an insurance policy rather than a response to concrete evidence.

US: the Fed is expected to hold on Wednesday even though Jefferson, Bowman and Waller signal another hike is likely but not urgent. Fed Chair Warsh did not talk up action at the IMF meetings. ING expects a December hike given strong growth, low unemployment and above-target inflation.
US 3Q GDP is expected at 3.4% annualised, driven by consumer spending and tech investment. Core PCE is expected to rise 0.3% m/m.
Bank of Canada is a close call on Wednesday. ING leans toward a hold given softer inflation, job losses and elevated unemployment in a 'risk off' environment, but expects a hike to come.
Eurozone 3Q GDP is expected near 0.3% q/q after 0.6% in 2Q, which was boosted by Irish data. Higher oil and gas prices likely weighed on October sentiment.

France 3Q GDP is expected to be flat after zero growth in 2Q and a 0.2% contraction in 1Q. Industrial production fell in July and August, goods consumption fell 0.5% in August, and rising rates, violence and protests weigh on confidence.

tension_points.bull_case: Hawks can point to the 3.8% September inflation, gas prices above the ECB's adverse scenario and the possibility of second-round effects. A December hike would act as insurance against a repeat of 2022.
tension_points.bear_case: The French fiscal and political crisis and higher bond yields argue for a hold. ING sees no concrete evidence yet of broader inflationary pressure and expects headline inflation to peak by spring.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence by spring that second-round effects in energy-intensive categories are materialising at scale would undermine ING's no-further-hikes view.
